h1: Working in a brewery warehouse and logistics team
title: Brewery Warehouse and Logistics Jobs | Craft Beer School
desc: What brewery warehouse and logistics staff do, why stock rotation and cold storage matter for beer and how to start in the role.
teaser: Beer can leave the brewery perfect and arrive tired. The warehouse and logistics team decides which.
standfirst: Warehouse and logistics jobs at a brewery are about more than moving cases. Beer is perishable, heavily taxed and easy to damage with heat. Here is what the work involves and why it is a solid way into the industry.
sections: Beer is a fresh product that travels badly

Most craft beer is unpasteurised and often unfiltered. It tastes best young and it stales faster when warm. Hop aroma fades, malt notes turn papery and the beer loses the character the brewers built. Heat and light are the two biggest enemies. Both are easy to find on an Indian highway in May.

The warehouse and logistics team is responsible for what happens between the packaging line and the outlet. They store finished beer, rotate stock, load trucks, track deliveries and handle returns. Done well, a guest in a bar 300 km away drinks the beer as the brewer intended. Done badly, the brewery takes the blame for something that happened on a loading dock.
The core jobs in a brewery warehouse

The work splits into a few areas:

  • Receiving. Checking incoming malt, hops, cans, bottles, labels and kegs against orders, then storing them correctly. Hops in particular need cold storage.
  • Finished goods storage. Keeping packaged beer cool, dry and out of light, stacked safely on pallets.
  • Stock rotation. First expired, first out, so older stock leaves before newer stock. In beer, this is non-negotiable.
  • Dispatch. Picking orders, loading vehicles and preparing the paperwork that goes with each load.
  • Kegs. Tracking where every keg is, collecting empties and sending them back for cleaning.
Excise paperwork is part of the job

Alcohol in India is a state subject, so every movement of beer is controlled and recorded. Breweries keep stock registers and need permits or passes for dispatches. The rules differ from one state to another. Warehouse staff do not need to be licensing experts, but they must record every case accurately. A count that does not match the register can create real trouble with excise officials.

Because rules vary by state and change over time, the brewery's compliance team or licensing adviser sets the procedure. The warehouse team's job is to follow it exactly and flag anything that does not add up.

A brewery's cold room is often kept at around 2 to 4 °C for kegs and fresh stock. Not every brewery can store all its packaged beer that cold, but cooler is always better than warmer. The worst damage tends to happen in transit and at outlets: a truck standing in the sun, cases stacked next to a kitchen, kegs left outside a bar.

Logistics staff can reduce that risk by planning loads for cooler hours, using insulated or refrigerated vehicles where the brewery has them and refusing to leave stock in unsafe conditions. Handling matters too. Cans dent, bottles break and kegs are heavy. A full 50 litre keg weighs well over 60 kg, so trolleys, proper lifting and forklift training are basic requirements.
Kegs are expensive and they go missing

Stainless steel kegs cost far more than the beer inside them. Every keg that goes to an outlet and does not come back is money gone. Good keg tracking, with numbered kegs, dispatch logs and regular reconciliation with customers, is one of the most valuable things a logistics team does.

Many breweries track kegs on a spreadsheet. Larger ones use barcodes or tracking software. Either way, the habit is the same: record every keg out, every keg back and chase the gap.

Returned kegs need care as well. Empties come back with beer residue that dries into a sticky film, which is hard to clean if it sits for weeks. Many breweries ask logistics to return kegs to the cellar promptly and to flag any that come back damaged, with missing spears or bent necks. A damaged keg that goes back into service can leak or fail to seal.

Logistics is a good entry point into a brewery because you see the whole operation from the output end. People move from the warehouse into production planning, supply chain, procurement or packaging. Some move into brewing, especially in smaller breweries where everyone helps on the line. Our guide to supply chain and procurement jobs covers the next step for many.

What makes the difference is understanding the product. A warehouse lead who knows why hoppy beer must ship cold and fast (and why a lager can sit a little longer) makes better calls than one following a rota. That brewing knowledge is the gap most warehouse staff have. It is also the easiest one to close.

Accuracy is the other quality that gets warehouse staff promoted. A picker who sends 48 cases instead of 50 creates an unhappy customer, a stock discrepancy and an excise record that no longer matches. Counting twice, signing for every load and logging breakages the same day are dull habits that make you trusted.

Your first step: ask your nearest brewery or distributor what temperature their finished beer is stored and shipped at, then note how many hours a typical delivery spends out of a cold room.
faqs: What does a brewery logistics team do?
It stores finished beer and raw materials, rotates stock, plans and loads deliveries, tracks kegs and keeps the stock records that excise rules require.
Why does beer need cold storage?
Most craft beer is unpasteurised and stales faster when warm. Cold storage slows the loss of hop aroma and the papery flavours that come with age.
Do warehouse staff need to know excise law?
They need to follow the brewery's procedures and keep accurate stock records. The rules vary by state, so the compliance team or a licensing adviser sets the process.
